item.title: Climatic Suitability and Invasion Risk of the Elm Zigzag Sawfly in North America
item.description:
相关度 59.3 · 关键词匹配：invasion risk、climatic suitability、uncertainty

The elm zigzag sawfly, Aproceros leucopoda (Hymenoptera), native to eastern Asia, is among the most concerning potential pests for elm trees (Ulmus spp.); elms form an important component in many North Temperate forests. This sawfly species invaded Europe in 2003 and spread rapidly across much of that continent. In 2020, it was recorded in North America, and it has since become established in several parts of the eastern United States and Canada. Sawfly infestations can cause severe elm tree defoliation, branch die-back that weakens tree health, and potentially tree mortality. Sawfly invasions have the potential to further exacerbate elm decline, especially in conjunction with other pressures, including Dutch elm disease (Ophiostoma ulmi). item.description:

The Nile grass rat ( Arvicanthis niloticus Desmarest, 1822) is one of the most destructive agricultural rodent pests and a primary reservoir host for multiple zoonotic pathogens in Egypt, including Schistosoma mansoni, Fasciola spp., Hymenolepis nana, murine typhus, and plague (Yersinia pestis via Xenopsylla cheopis fleas). Quantifying how ongoing climate change will alter its potential geographic distribution is essential for national rodent control strategies and vector-borne disease surveillance. item.description:

Conservation planning for squamates is frequently constrained by their cryptic ecology and by the rare species conservation paradox, whereby limited distribution data restricts the development of effective management strategies. We focus on Lacertoides pardalis , a narrow endemic skink restricted to ultramafic substrates in New Caledonia, where suitable habitats are increasingly fragmented by nickel mining and recurrent wildfires. To overcome data limitations, we combined ensembles of small models with Bayesian additive regression trees to model habitat suitability using a parsimonious set of bioclimatic variables and a remotely sensed vegetation index (NDVI). item.description:

Stevia rebaudiana (Bertoni) Bertoni is a South American crop of increasing agronomic relevance because its leaves accumulate steviol glycosides, high-intensity natural sweeteners used as low-calorie alternatives to sucrose. Although the species is native to Paraguay and adjacent regions, its cultivation has expanded beyond its native range, making the identification of suitable growing areas relevant for agricultural planning under climate change. Here, we modelled the current and future environmental suitability for S. rebaudiana cultivation in South America using cultivation records, bioclimatic variables, and soil predictors. item.title: Projecting the potential distribution of sea buckthorn in the Hindu Kush Himalaya under climate change using ensemble species distribution modelling
item.description:
相关度 70.1 · 关键词匹配：species distribution modelling、habitat suitability、potential distribution

Sea Buckthorn is a multipurpose shrub valued for its nutrient-rich berries, land aggradation ability, and support to livelihoods in high-altitude regions. However, rapid environmental changes are threatening its habitats. Despite its climatic vulnerability, the impact of climate change on its habitats is poorly understood in the Hindu Kush Himalayas (HKH), a region spanning across eight countries. This critical gap was addressed by a macroecological assessment of the current and projected habitat suitability of H. rhamnoides , H. salicifolia , and H. tibetana across the HKH. item.description:

Cupressus funebris , an indigenous and ecologically important conifer in China, is increasingly endangered by climate change and habitat fragmentation. Using an ensemble species distribution model (BIOMOD2), we projected current and future habitat suitability under three climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5) for the 2050s, 2070s, and 2090s. We integrated 355 occurrence records and bioclimatic variables using 12 algorithms. We also used the InVEST Habitat Quality model to assess current habitat quality and degradation, and constructed an ecological security pattern from habitat patches and resistance surfaces. This framework identified climate refugia and priority conservation zones. Random Forest performed best (AUC = 0.92 ± 0.02, TSS = 0.85 ± 0.03). The desert mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus crooki) is distributed throughout the southern United States and northern Mexico. As a large herbivore, this subspecies plays a crucial role in maintaining ecological balance. While its distribution is closely linked to water availability and vegetation type, climate change is increasingly altering these factors and shifting potential habitats. This study aimed to model the current potential distribution of O. h. crooki and predict distribution changes for the 2021–2040 period in relation to bioclimatic factors. Presence data were compiled from multiple sources, including GBIF, nocturnal sightings, pellet counts, and camera traps. These records were correlated with 19 bioclimatic variables from WorldClim. item.description:
相关度 71.7 · 关键词匹配：species distribution model、maxent、distribution model

Species distribution model (SDM) have become important tools for biodiversity assessment, ecological prediction, and conservation planning. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have expanded their capacity to analyse complex ecological data. However, the overall development trajectory, knowledge structure, and methodological implications of machine learning-based SDM (ML-SDM) remain insufficiently synthesized. This study provides a systematic overview of ML-SDM research from 2006 to 2025 by integrating bibliometric analysis with methodological synthesis. item.title: Bayesian Wombling for Tracking Invasive Species
item.description:
相关度 56.7 · 关键词匹配：invasive species、uncertainty

This paper develops Bayesian wombling, or boundary analysis for tracking invasive species. We focus on three invasive species of concern in North America: Lycorma delicatula, Adelges tsugae, and Microstegium vimineum. We aim to demonstrate the applicability of wombling for supporting invasive pest management activities. In spatial science wombling is used widely to track regions of rapid change within the spatial reference domain. We use Gaussian process models for point-referenced spatial data followed by predictive inference on rates of change over curves using line integrals. We extend the wombling model based Bayesian inference framework to feature simple analytic forms that avoid high dimensional quadrature while offering uncertainty quantification over curvilinear spatial boundaries.

Climate change, biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation, and the increasing frequency of environmental hazards have created an urgent need for intelligent, data-driven environmental monitoring systems. Traditional monitoring approaches often face limitations related to spatial coverage, temporal resolution, data integration, operational cost, and the ability to identify complex environmental patterns. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, geospatial analytics, cloud computing, and big data platforms offer opportunities to improve environmental observation, prediction, and decision-making. An R workflow that tests whether an invasive aquatic plant has filled its potential range, and translates the answer into catchment-level management zones. It is applied to Nuttall’s waterweed (Elodea nuttallii), an invasive alien species of Union concern, and its long-established congener Elodea canadensis in Germany. A single script runs every step, from raw GBIF downloads to figures, tables and maps, and writes an audit trail as it goes. The workflow first cleans GBIF records of seven aquatic macrophytes with identical filters (location in Germany, coordinate uncertainty of 10 km or less, collection year 1980 or later, one record per species and location) and thins them spatially. Species distribution models (SDMs) are essential tools for predicting the impacts of climate change on biodiversity. However, their predictive performance remains strongly scale-dependent, posing a persistent challenge in biogeography. Particularly, the combined effects of spatial extent and resolution on model transferability and ecological interpretability remain poorly understood. item.description:

Intensified globalisation and the movement of plant materials have increased pathways for plant invasions and the risk of plant disease establishment globally. Mango bacterial black spot (MBBS) is an invasive disease native to Africa. The disease poses a serious threat to global mango production and trade. Yet MBBS habitat‐suitability models that can guide surveillance and monitoring programmes remain poorly documented. This study predicts global climate‐suitable areas for MBBS using the Maximum Entropy model. Future projections were conducted under two socioeconomic pathways (SSPs245 and 585) and two time periods (2050s: 2041–2060 and 2070s: 2061–2080). The models showed strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.890, TSS = 0.686, and CBI = 0.705). Whether invasive species conserve their ancestral climatic niches or undergo realized niche changes during global spread fundamentally affects the reliability of invasion risk projections. We integrated ensemble species distribution models (SDMs), the extended COUE framework, and Multivariate Environmental Similarity Surfaces (MESS) to quantify the global climatic niche dynamics and invasion risk of Solanum rostratum Dunal (Solanaceae) across its native North America and four invaded regions. Macroecological modeling revealed a temperature-driven, precipitation-constrained distribution, where thermal availability and mean diurnal range dictated suitability, while precipitation extremes imposed strict limits. This study evaluates the relationship between MaxEnt-predicted habitat suitability and departmental estimates of population density for 14 game mammal species in the Pavlodar Region. Model performance varied substantially among species (Test AUC = 0.538-0.992; TSS = 0.220-0.984), and extremely high AUC values for some species with small samples were interpreted cautiously. For 41 territorial units, habitat suitability was aggregated as the mean MaxEnt value within each polygon and compared with density using Spearman's rank correlation.
